query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Hf and Al2O3 to a MoSi2 coating can improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: MoSi2 coating on a Mo-based alloy substrate
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide scale containing HfO2, SiO2, and mullite
generation.mechanism: The oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, reducing the oxidation rate of the coating
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, with a reduced mass gain rate after 40 h of oxidation
generation.baseline: MoSi2 coating without Hf and Al2O3 co-doping
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 400-600 °C, where MoSi2 suffers from rapid pesting oxidation
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the synthetic reactions between Al2O3, HfO2, and SiO2 is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Isothermal oxidation test at 1400 °C in static air
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the co-doped coating exhibits a higher mass gain rate or a less protective oxide scale than the undoped coating, the hypothesis is falsified

Among them, MoSi2 has attracted much attention due to its high melting point (2030 °C), moderate density of 6.24 g/cm3, and similar CTE (8.1 × 10−6/°C) to refractory metals (e.g., Mo 6.7 × 10−6/°C). In addition, it performs limited protective performance at higher temperatures due to the volatilization of SiO2, which has hindered its use under high-temperature oxidizing environments [,]. Attempts have been made to introduce alloying elements such as aluminum (Al), titanium (Ti), zirconium (Zr), and hafnium (Hf), as well as their oxides (e.g., Al2O3, ZrO2, HfO2), into MoSi2-based coatings to enhance their properties at elevated temperatures [,,,,,,]. Hf has been widely adopted to improve the high-temperature performance of superalloys [,,,] (e.g., Ni-, Co-, Fe-, and Nb-based superalloys) and the high-temperature coatings on those superalloy substrates (e.g., β-NiAl coating with B2 structure [], aluminide coating [], AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coating []).

In this work, Hf and Al2O3 were co-doped to a MoSi2 coating to form a new (Mo,Hf)Si2-Al2O3 composite coating on a Mo-based alloy substrate. Among the various coating techniques to prepare MoSi2-based silicide coatings on refractory metals, vacuum slurry sintering is probably the most competitive, which offers the advantages of being low-cost, effective, and easy to operate [,]. Moreover, a metallurgical bond between the coating and substrate can be expected. Accordingly, the Hf-Al2O3 co-doped MoSi2 coating was fabricated on a Mo-based substrate by the method of slurry sintering. The isothermal oxidation behavior of the composite coating was evaluated at 1400 °C in static air. Figure 4 shows a schematic diagram of the microstructure evolution of the composite coating during preparation. The slurry containing Si, Mo, Hf, and Al2O3 powders was sprayed onto the surface of the Mo-based alloy substrate and then sintered at 1480 °C. Since the sintering temperature was above its melting point (1410 °C), Si was in a molten state and diffused inward to the direction of the matrix and reacted with the Mo-based substrate to form a Mo-silicide inner layer by liquid phase reaction, resulting in a relatively dense structure. High melting point elements Mo and Hf had a much slower inward diffusion rate and mainly enriched in the outer layer to form (Mo,Hf)Si2 phases, as shown in Figure 3a,d. At the same time, the solid Al2O3 particle would not participate in the chemical reaction and was distributed between the sintering reaction products on the coating surface, forming a relatively loose (Mo,Hf)Si2-Al2O3 outer layer on the surface, as shown in Figure 3a,e,f. The revealed regularities of oxidation of the coating were attributed to the oxidation behavior during oxidation. In the initial stage, the coating oxidized, and the oxide scale (containing, e.g., HfO2, SiO2) was formed on the coating surface, resulting in rapid weight gain of the coating. However, the oxide scale was insufficient to wrap the substrate; consequently, significant oxidative weight gain was observed in Stage I. In Stage II, a relatively dense oxide scale was formed on the coating surface with an oxidation time extension. Since a protective oxide scale formed on the surface of the coating, the oxidation rate was under the control of the permeation of oxygen through the dense oxide scale, thus the mass gain rate decreased.
